newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Lonrho wants to stick to platinum.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Lonrho wants to stick to platinum.

text.p: International conglomerate Lonrho Plc, in which South Africa's Anglo American Corp has a 28 percent stake, said on Thursday it wants to stick to its platinum operations.
"We have no intention to sell our platinum business," Lonrho's chief executive Nick Morrell told Reuters.
Morrell's commments come as the European Commission is conducting a probe into the competition complications of Anglo's stake in Lonrho.

Both companies are major producers of platinum which is used in car exhaust catalysts. The EU earlier barred Lonrho from merging its platinum operations with Anglo's South African rival Gencor, which has appealed.
"It is an Anglo or a Gencor problem if you like," said Morrell. "We intend to make our future as an independent company producing platinum. What that does to Anglo or Gencor is not Lonrho's issue."
There had been market speculation that Anglo wanted Lonrho to dispose of its platinum assets, but this was denied by Morrell.
"I have had no such suggestion," said Morrell, adding that relations with Anglo, Lonrho's biggest single shareholder were "good and cordial".
The EU has barred Anglo from voting its Lonrho shares pending its investigation, but this was no obstacle in Lonrho's plan to separate its mining and non-mining business.
"The fact they cannot vote their shares has no bearing on our programme," said Morrell.
"It won't stop me from going to shareholders and asking them for permission to do something in terms of a demerger or a sale," Morrell added.
A demerger, preceded by the sale of the Princess hotels chain, was the preferred route to separate the mining business from the African trading operations, Morrell said.
But he declined to say when Lonrho expected the Princess divestment or the planned demerger to be completed.
Neither did he want to confirm press reports that Lonrho is negotiating the Princess divestment with Saudi Prince al-Waleed bin Talal.
Pointing to possible regulatory hurdles, Morrell also stressed that it was not sure yet whether a demerger would actually take place.
"Whether we can achieve a demerger, I don't yet know, but I think it is the obvious route for giving shareholders maximum value," he said.
